claims.claim: Transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components.
claims.source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components and that mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced this association (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced the association with eIF4F components.
claims.source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that transfection of GFP-tagged versions of either the MNV or NV VPg proteins into 293 T cells allowed for the affinity purification of eIF4F components and that mutations in the eIF4G binding domain of VPg reduced this association (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing wild-type and mutant VPg proteins.

claims.claim: Most of the proteins identified by quantitative mass spectrometry of VPg-associated complexes were components of the host cell translation complex including ribosomal proteins, translation initiation factors and host RNA binding proteins.
claims.source: Most of the proteins identified were components of the host cell translation complex including ribosomal proteins, translation initiation factors and host RNA binding proteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 1D and supplementary files.

claims.claim: hnRNPA1 was identified in VPg-associated complexes and has been previously shown to act in norovirus genome circularization.
claims.source: In addition, we identified hnRNPA1 which we have previously shown to act in norovirus genome circularization (López-Manríquez et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on hnRNPA1 function.

claims.claim: YBX1, DDX3 and several other proteins that previously interact with the 5' end of the viral RNA were enriched on VPg.
claims.source: YBX1, DDX3 and several other proteins that we have previously found to interact with the 5' end of the viral RNA (Vashist et al., 2012a) were also enriched on VPg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on 5' RNA binding proteins.

claims.claim: The association of all proteins tested except YBX1 were reduced by the introduction of eIF4G-binding site mutations into the MNV VPg protein.
claims.source: Except for YBX1, the association of all proteins tested were reduced by the introduction of eIF4G-binding site mutations into the MNV VPg protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The norovirus VPg proteins interact with a complex network of host factors, many of which have been implicated in the host cell translation initiation process.
claims.source: Together, these data extend our previous observations and confirm that the norovirus VPg proteins interact with a complex network of host factors, many of which have been implicated in the host cell translation initiation process.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined proteomic and western blot data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Silver stain of the purified complexes from FLAG-tagged virus infections confirmed the presence of the bait proteins, with both the uncleaved and cleaved forms of NS1/2 and NS2 being highly enriched.
claims.source: Silver stain of the purified complexes confirmed the presence of the bait proteins, with both the uncleaved and cleaved forms of NS1/2 and NS2 being highly enriched (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by silver stain data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Complexes purified from NS1/2-Flag virus infected cells co-purified untagged NS4 and vice versa.
claims.source: As expected, complexes purified from NS1/2-Flag virus infected cells co-purified untagged NS4 and vice versa (Figure 2B), as we have previously shown these proteins to interact to form a complex (Thorne et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by silver stain data in Figure 2B and cites previous work on NS1/2-NS4 interaction.

claims.claim: Western blot analysis of the purified complexes confirmed that viral non-structural and structural proteins were specifically enriched in the purified complexes, including NS5 (VPg)-containing precursors.
claims.source: Western blot analysis of the purified complexes confirmed that viral non-structural and structural proteins were specifically enriched in the purified complexes, including NS5 (VPg)-containing precursors (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: All viral proteins, including the VF1 protein product of ORF4, were enriched in the viral replication complex.
claims.source: As expected, all viral proteins, including the VF1 protein product of ORF4, an innate immune antagonist (McFadden et al., 2011), were enriched in the viral replication complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on VF1 function.

claims.claim: There was a significant correlation between the relative enrichment of proteins identified using NS1/2 and NS4 (Spearman correlation of 0.8832).
claims.source: There was a significant correlation between the relative enrichment of proteins identified using NS1/2 and NS4 (Spearman correlation of 0.8832), fitting with our prior knowledge that both proteins form a complex during viral replication (Thorne et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on NS1/2-NS4 complex formation.

claims.claim: Ontology analysis indicated that proteins involved in vesicle transport and fatty acid metabolism were significantly enriched in the replication complex.
claims.source: Ontology analysis indicated that proteins involved in vesicle transport and fatty acid metabolism were significantly enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3), fitting with previous observations that the viral replication complex is associated with cytoplasmic membranous structures (Cotton et al., 2017; Hyde and Mackenzie, 2010; Hyde et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on replication complex membrane association.

claims.claim: VapA and the paralogue VapB, which bind to the NS1/2 protein, were both highly enriched in the replication complex.
claims.source: We noted that the VapA and the paralogue VapB, which we have recently identified as binding to the NS1/2 protein (McCune et al., 2017), were both highly enriched.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cites previous work on VapA/VapB-NS1/2 interaction.

claims.claim: NS4 failed to enrich mature VPg, instead purifying only the polyprotein cleavage intermediate NS4/5(VPg).
claims.source: We observed that NS4 failed to enrich mature VPg, instead purifying only the polyprotein cleavage intermediate NS4/5(VPg) (Figure 2C and S2.2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: NS1/2 effectively pulled down mature VPg.
claims.source: In contrast, NS1/2 effectively pulled down mature VPg (Figure 2C and S2.2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment.
claims.source: Consistent with this, NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment, likely indicating that the NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation.
claims.source: Consistent with this, NS1/2 enriched the VPg binding partner eIF4G more than 2-fold, while pulldown of NS4 resulted in no eIF4G enrichment, likely indicating that the NS4/5 (VPg) precursor cannot effectively function in translation initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NS4/5(VPg) does not enrich eIF4G, combined with knowledge that eIF4G binding is required for VPg-dependent translation.

claims.claim: Binding of C-terminal VPg fusion proteins to eIF4G is inhibited.
claims.source: This is consistent with a previous observation that binding of C-terminal VPg fusion proteins to eIF4G is inhibited (Leen et al., 2016), but may further suggest that the function of VPg is also altered when present as an N-terminal fusion with NS4.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Leen et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Most host factors identified using VPg were enriched by >2 fold using only the NS1/2 tagged virus, and not the NS4-tagged virus.
claims.source: Consistent with our observations with the well-established VPg partner eIF4G, most host factors identified using VPg were enriched by >2 fold using only the NS1/2 tagged virus, and not the NS4-tagged virus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of mass spectrometry data from VPg, NS1/2, and NS4 pulldowns.

claims.claim: G3BP1 was enriched by VPg, NS1/2, and NS4.
claims.source: One protein was enriched by VPg, NS1/2, and NS4 – the core stress granule protein G3BP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In the CRISPR screen, the MNV receptor Cd300lf was the most highly positively selected gene identified.
claims.source: In both screens, the MNV receptor Cd300lf was the most highly positively selected gene identified, in agreement with previous reports (Haga et al., 2016; Orchard et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous reports identifying Cd300lf as the MNV receptor.

claims.claim: The previously characterised pro-viral MNV gene VapA was identified in both CRISPR screens.
claims.source: The previously characterised pro-viral MNV gene VapA (McCune et al., 2017) was also identified in both screens (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous work characterizing VapA.

claims.claim: G3BP1 was the second most highly enriched gene in the CRISPR screen.
claims.source: The second most highly enriched gene was G3BP1, a gene also identified in one of the two previous CRISPR screens performed on norovirus infected cells (Orchard et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites a previous CRISPR screen.

claims.claim: Comparing the CRISPR data obtained using two divergent strains of MNV showed 89 common pro-viral hits and five common anti-viral hits.
claims.source: Comparing the CRISPR data obtained in this study using two divergent strains of MNV showed a high degree of overlap, with 89 common pro-viral hit and five common anti-viral hits (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR screen data from CW3 and CR6 strains.

claims.claim: Four genes were identified as common proviral hits across all CRISPR screens: CD300lf, G3BP1, Kmt2d, and Smarce1.
claims.source: However comparison with the previous reported CRISPR screen used to identify the MNV receptor (Orchard et al., 2016) showed only seven proviral hits for CW3 and 8 for CR6, of which only four were common for both strains across all screens (Supplementary file 4). The four genes identified were the MNV receptor CD300lf, the stress granule component G3BP1, the histone methytransferase Kmt2d and Smarce1, which encodes an actin dependent regulator of chromatin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of CRISPR screen data across multiple studies.

claims.claim: Pathway over-representation analysis of the pro-viral genes identified in the CRISPR screens highlighted mRNA processing, RNA splicing and methylation as the three most highly represented gene ontology terms.
claims.source: Pathway over-representation analysis (Liao et al., 2019) of the genes pro-viral genes identified in the CRISPR screens performed in this study highlighted mRNA processing, RNA splicing and methylation as the three most highly represented gene ontology (GO) terms (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of CRISPR screen data.

claims.claim: PTBP1 was one of the genes identified in the enriched GO terms and has been previously shown to bind to a 3' pyrimidine-rich stretch in the MNV genome which is important for viral pathogenesis.
claims.source: The gene encoding PTBP1, polypyrimidine tract binding protein, was one of the genes identified in these enriched GO terms. PTBP1 is a protein we have previously shown to bind to a 3' pyrimidine-rich stretch in the MNV genome which is important for viral pathogenesis (Bailey et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous work on PTBP1 function.

claims.claim: G3BP1 was identified in all three screens (VPg proteomics, replication complex proteomics, and CRISPR) as a potential host factor essential for norovirus infection.
claims.source: A cross-comparison of the data obtained from all three approaches allowed us to identify several host proteins that were common to all screens (Supplementary file 5). G3BP1, the core stress granule component was identified in all three screens as a potential host factor essential for norovirus infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from all three experimental approaches.

claims.claim: A clear defect was observed in the ability to replicate and produce infectious virus in three independently selected ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
claims.source: A clear defect was observed in the ability to replicate to produce infectious virus in three independently selected ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The inability of MNV to replicate in ΔG3BP1 cells was mirrored by an inability to induce cytopathic effect leading to virus-induced cell death.
claims.source: This effect was mirrored by an inability to induce cytopathic effect leading to virus-induced cell death (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The ability of encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) to infect and cause cell death was unaffected by the deletion of G3BP1.
claims.source: In contrast, the ability of encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) to infect and cause cell death was unaffected by the deletion of G3BP1 (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect data shown in Figure 4C and D comparing MNV and EMCV infection.

claims.claim: Cells lacking G3BP1 are highly resistant to norovirus infection.
claims.source: These data confirm that cells lacking G3BP1 are highly resistant to norovirus infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing defects in MNV replication and cytopathic effect in ΔG3BP1 cells.

claims.claim: Transfection of replicon RNA, purified from replicon containing cells, into BHK cells readily resulted in the formation of antibiotic resistant cell colonies.
claims.source: Transfection of replicon RNA, purified from replicon containing cells, into BHK cells readily resulted in the formation of antibiotic resistant cell colonies (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: RNA that was proteinase K treated prior to transfection was unable to produce replicon containing colonies.
claims.source: In contrast, RNA that was proteinase K treated prior to transfection was unable to produce replicon containing colonies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A comparing untreated and proteinase K treated RNA.

claims.claim: CRISPR modified U2OS cells that lacked G3BP1 were unable to support NV replication, as evident by the lack of antibiotic resistant colonies.
claims.source: CRISPR modified U2OS cells that lacked G3BP1 (Kedersha et al., 2016) were unable to support NV replication, as evident by the lack of antibiotic resistant colonies (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5B and cites the source of the G3BP1 knockout cells.

claims.claim: While a significant increase in NV viral RNA levels was seen in WT U2OS cells, those lacking G3BP1 were completely unable to support NV RNA synthesis.
claims.source: While a significant increase in NV viral RNA levels was seen in WT U2OS cells, those lacking G3BP1 were completely unable to support NV RNA synthesis (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the absence of G3BP1 the formation of antibiotic resistant microcolonies was completely ablated and then subsequently restored in ΔG3BP1 cells engineered to express the wild type version of G3BP1.
claims.source: In the absence of G3BP1 the formation of antibiotic resistant microcolonies was completely ablated and then subsequently restored in ΔG3BP1 cells engineered to express the wild type version of G3BP1 (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5D comparing WT, ΔG3BP1, and complemented cells.

claims.claim: G3BP1 is essential for human Norwalk virus replication.
claims.source: These data indicate that like for MNV, G3BP1 is essential for human Norwalk virus replication.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing defects in NV replication in G3BP1 knockout cells.

claims.claim: Complementation with full length murine G3BP1 restored the ability of MNV to induce cell death back to near wild type levels.
claims.source: Complementation with full length murine G3BP1 restored the ability of MNV to induce cell death (Figure 6B) and to produce infectious virus (Figure 6C) back to near wild type levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: Complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation.
claims.source: In contrast, complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation, and deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C comparing different G3BP1 truncations.

claims.claim: Deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity.
claims.source: In contrast, complementation with a variant carrying a deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation, and deletion of both the RGG and RRM domains together resulted in complete loss of complementation capacity (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cytopathic effect and virus yield data shown in Figure 6B and 6C comparing different G3BP1 truncations.

claims.claim: The RNA binding domains of G3BP1 are essential for its function in the norovirus life cycle.
claims.source: These data confirm that the RNA binding domains of G3BP1 are essential for its function in the norovirus life cycle.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments showing that deletion of RNA binding domains abolishes G3BP1 function.

claims.claim: The levels of infectivity obtained following transfection of ΔG3BP1 cell lines with MNV viral RNA was comparable to that obtained in WT cells in the presence of the nucleoside analogue 2'-C-methylcytidin (2CMC).
claims.source: The levels of infectivity obtained following transfection of ΔG3BP1 cell lines with MNV viral RNA was comparable to that obtained in WT cells in the presence of the nucleoside analogue 2'-C-methylcytidin (2CMC), a known inhibitor of the norovirus RNA polymerase (Rocha-Pereira et al., 2012; Rocha-Pereira et al., 2013) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by virus yield data shown in Figure 7A and cites previous work on 2CMC as a polymerase inhibitor.

claims.claim: No viral proteins were detected in either of the ΔG3BP1 cell lines following transfection of VPg-linked RNA, suggesting a defect at a very early stage in the viral life cycle.
claims.source: No viral proteins were detected in either of the ΔG3BP1 cell lines suggesting a defect at a very early stage in the viral life cycle (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and represents an inference about the stage of the life cycle affected.

claims.claim: Transfection of VPg-linked RNA into the ΔG3BP1 cell lines reconstituted with WT G3BP1 restored the ability to produce infectious virus and viral proteins.
claims.source: Transfection of VPg-linked RNA into the ΔG3BP1 cell lines reconstituted with WT G3BP1 restored the ability to produce infectious virus (Figure 7B) and the production of viral proteins (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by virus yield and western blot data shown in Figure 7B and 7D.

claims.claim: G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle.
claims.source: These data confirm that G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle and that in the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from RNA transfection experiments that bypass the entry step.

claims.claim: In the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
claims.source: These data confirm that G3BP1 is required for a post entry stage of the norovirus life cycle and that in the absence of G3BP1 no norovirus replication was observed within the sensitivity of the assay used.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the lack of detectable viral proteins and infectious virus in ΔG3BP1 cells.

claims.claim: The production of viral positive sense RNA was reduced to background levels in the absence of G3BP1, comparable to levels observed when 2CMC was present during the infection.
claims.source: The production of viral positive sense RNA was reduced to background levels in the absence of G3BP1, comparable to levels observed when the 2CMC was present during the infection (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Viral negative sense RNA synthesis was reduced to below the detection limit of the assay in ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
claims.source: Viral negative sense RNA synthesis was also reduced to below the detection limit of the assay in ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: An ~5 fold increase in viral negative sense RNA production was detected at 6 hr post infection of WT cells in the presence of 2CMC, likely representing the first round of viral negative sense RNA synthesis.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we were able to detect an ~5 fold increase in viral negative sense RNA production at 6 hr post infection of WT cells in the presence of 2CMC, which, given that 2CMC was added after the inoculation phase (Figure 8B), likely represents the first round of viral negative sense RNA synthesis, confirming the sensitivity of the assay.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C and represents an interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: Viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis was near (or below) the sensitivity of the assay following transfection of viral VPg-linked RNA into two independent ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
claims.source: Similar results were obtained following transfection of viral RNA into cells to bypass the entry phase; viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis was near (or below) the sensitivity of the assay following transfection of viral VPg-linked RNA into two independent ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 8D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claims.claim: Complementation with WT G3BP1, but not the mutant forms lacking the RNA binding domains, restored viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis.
claims.source: Complementation with WT G3BP1, but not the mutant forms lacking the RNA binding domains, also restored viral positive and negative sense RNA synthesis (Figure 8F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8F and G comparing complementation with different G3BP1 variants.

claims.claim: The function of G3BP1 is prior to, or at the level of viral negative sense RNA synthesis.
claims.source: Together these data suggest that the function of G3BP1 is prior to, or at the level of viral negative sense RNA synthesis, with the most logical steps being either viral RNA translation or the formation of viral replication complexes.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNA synthesis data showing defects at the level of negative strand synthesis.

claims.claim: The norovirus VPg proteins form a complex that contains multiple components of the large and small ribosomal subunits.
claims.source: Our proteomics analysis also confirms that the norovirus VPg proteins form a complex that contains multiple components of the large and small ribosomal subunits (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: G3BP1 associates with 40S subunits.
claims.source: It has been established previously that G3BP1 associates with 40S subunits (Kedersha et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: GFP-tagged WT MNV VPg was readily able to pull down eIF4G, G3BP1 and RpS6, a component of the 40S subunit.
claims.source: GFP-tagged WT MNV VPg was readily able to pull down eIF4G, G3BP1 and RpS6, a component of the 40S subunit (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: In the absence of G3BP1, the ability to pull down RpS6 and RpS3 was lost.
claims.source: However, in the absence of G3BP1, the ability to pull down RpS6 and RpS3 was lost (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Disruption of the VPg-eIF4G interaction by the introduction of the F123A mutation significantly reduced the ability to pull down RpS6, RpS3, and RpL4.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that disruption of the VPg-eIF4G interaction by the introduction of the F123A mutation into the eIF4G binding domain, also significantly reduced the ability to pull down RpS6, RpS3, as well as RpL4, a component of the large ribosomal subunit (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Upon reconstitution of G3BP1 expression, the levels of RpS6, RpS3 and RpL4 associated with VPg were enhanced.
claims.source: We also observed that upon reconstitution of G3BP1 expression, the levels of RpS6, RpS3 and RpL4 associated with VPg were enhanced (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the absence of G3BP1, the amount of viral RNA associated with the ribosomal subunit protein RpS3 was decreased.
claims.source: We found that in the absence of G3BP1, the amount of viral RNA associated with the ribosomal subunit protein RpS3 was decreased (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-IP data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: G3BP1 likely contributes in some manner to the association of VPg and viral VPg-linked RNA with ribosomal subunits.
claims.source: These data suggest that that G3BP1 likely contributes in some manner to the association of VPg and viral VPg-linked RNA with ribosomal subunits.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the GFP-Trap and RNA-IP data showing reduced ribosome association in the absence of G3BP1.

claims.claim: Even in the presence of 2CMC, which inhibits viral RNA synthesis, there was a small but measurable increase in free 80S ribosomes over time in WT cells but not in cells lacking G3BP1.
claims.source: We noted that even in the presence of 2CMC, which inhibits viral RNA synthesis, there was a small but measurable increase in free 80S ribosomes over time in WT cells but not in cells lacking G3BP1 (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: MNV infection results in translation shut off and this effect is at least partially due to the activity of the NS6 protease.
claims.source: We have previously found that MNV infection results in translation shut off and that this effect is at least partially due to the activity of the NS6 protease (Emmott et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: While most ribosome-associated norovirus RNA in WT cells was found in polysomes containing fractions, less viral RNA was found in ribosome-containing fractions in the absence of G3BP1.
claims.source: Further analyses indicated that while most ribosome-associated norovirus RNA in WT cells was found in polysomes containing fractions, less viral RNA was found in ribosome-containing fractions (1–12 in Figure 10A and B) in the absence of G3BP1 and, in comparison to WT cells, very little viral RNA was found in fractions containing polysomes (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling and viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claims.claim: In the absence of G3BP1 norovirus RNA is less efficient at assembling into polysomal fractions, suggesting a defect at the level of viral protein synthesis.
claims.source: Extending the fractionation to include the free RNA and ribonucleoprotein complexes at the top of each gradient confirmed that in the absence of G3BP1 norovirus RNA is less efficient at assembling into polysomal fractions, suggesting a defect at the level of viral protein synthesis (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by extended polysome profiling data shown in Figure 10C and represents an interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: G3BP1 functions to promote the translation of norovirus VPg-linked RNA, by facilitating the association with ribosomal subunits and the formation of polysomes on viral RNA.
claims.source: Together these data support the hypothesis that G3BP1 functions to promote the translation of norovirus VPg-linked RNA, by facilitating the association with ribosomal subunits and the formation of polysomes on viral RNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the polysome profiling data showing reduced polysome association in the absence of G3BP1.

claims.claim: Both cap-dependent and CrPV IRES-dependent translation were comparable in extracts prepared from WT and ΔG3BP1 cell lines.
claims.source: Both cap-dependent (Figure 11B) and CrPV IRES-dependent translation (Figure 11C) were comparable in extracts prepared from WT and ΔG3BP1 cell lines (Figure 11A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11B and C.

claims.claim: Norovirus VPg-dependent translation was reduced in nuclease treated extracts prepared from cells lacking G3BP.
claims.source: We found that norovirus VPg-dependent translation was reduced in nuclease treated extracts prepared from cells lacking G3BP (Figure 11D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11D.

claims.claim: Translation in nuclease treated extracts was on average reduced by ~40–50% because of G3BP1 ablation.
claims.source: Quantification of the levels of multiple viral proteins produced over multiple experiments indicated that translation in nuclease treated extracts was on average reduced by ~40–50% because of G3BP1 ablation (Figure 11E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11E.

claims.claim: A 50% reduction in translation efficiency was consistently observed in extracts that were not nuclease treated, and therefore contained physiologically relevant levels of cellular mRNAs.
claims.source: This 50% reduction in translation efficiency was also consistently observed in extracts that were not nuclease treated, and therefore contained physiologically relevant levels of cellular mRNAs (Figure 11F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation data shown in Figure 11F and G.

claims.claim: G3BP1 functions to enhance norovirus VPg-dependent translation initiation.
claims.source: These data further confirm that G3BP1 functions to enhance norovirus VPg-dependent translation initiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro translation data showing reduced translation in the absence of G3BP1.

claims.claim: G3BP1 plays a key role in the processes of norovirus VPg-dependent protein synthesis.
claims.source: Furthermore, we determined that G3BP1 plays a key role in the processes of norovirus VPg-dependent protein synthesis, uncovering a new function for G3BP1 in facilitating RNA virus genome translation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The combined approaches resulted in the identification of the core stress granule component G3BP1 as a host protein critical for the replication of both murine and human noroviruses in cell culture.
claims.source: Our combined approaches resulted in the identification of the core stress granule component G3BP1 as a host protein critical for the replication of both murine and human noroviruses in cell culture.

results.result: Norovirus VPg proteins interact with the eIF4F translation initiation complex and multiple host translation factors. VPg contains a conserved C-terminal domain that binds eIF4G via a conserved phenylalanine residue, and this interaction is required for association with other translation factors including ribosomal proteins, eIF3 subunits, and RNA binding proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (m7-GTP affinity purification, GFP-Trap immunoprecipitation, quantitative mass spectrometry, and western blotting) demonstrating VPg interactions with translation machinery. The data show both wild-type and mutant VPg proteins in authentic replication contexts and overexpression systems, with consistent results across MNV and human NV. The requirement for the eIF4G binding domain is demonstrated by reduced associations in F123A/F137A mutants.

results.result: The MNV replication complex proteome was characterized using FLAG-tagged NS1/2 and NS4 proteins during authentic viral infection. The replication complex contains all viral proteins and is enriched for host factors involved in vesicle transport, fatty acid metabolism, and membrane organization, consistent with the membrane-associated nature of norovirus replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C19 describe a comprehensive proteomic analysis using SILAC labeling and FLAG-tagged viruses with appropriate controls. The silver stain, western blot, and mass spectrometry data (Figure 2) demonstrate specific enrichment of viral and host proteins. The high correlation between NS1/2 and NS4 pulldowns (Spearman 0.8832) and gene ontology analysis support the conclusions. Previous findings (VapA/VapB, NS1/2-NS4 interaction) validate the approach.

results.result: NS1/2 and NS4 differentially enrich VPg and translation factors during infection. NS1/2 enriches mature VPg and eIF4G, while NS4 only enriches the NS4/5(VPg) precursor without eIF4G, suggesting the uncleaved precursor cannot function in translation initiation. G3BP1 was uniquely enriched by both NS1/2 and NS4 as well as VPg.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 are supported by western blot and mass spectrometry data comparing NS1/2 and NS4 pulldowns (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The differential enrichment of mature VPg vs. NS4/5(VPg) precursor is clearly shown, and the lack of eIF4G enrichment by NS4 is consistent with previous work (C24) showing C-terminal fusions inhibit eIF4G binding. The unique enrichment of G3BP1 by all three baits is a key observation.

results.result: A genome-wide CRISPR screen using two MNV strains (CW3 and CR6) identified host factors required for norovirus infection. The MNV receptor Cd300lf and G3BP1 were the top two hits, with 89 common pro-viral genes between strains. Gene ontology analysis highlighted mRNA processing, RNA splicing, and methylation as enriched pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 describe a well-controlled CRISPR screen with biological validation through use of two viral strains and comparison with previous screens. The identification of known factors (Cd300lf, VapA) validates the approach. The 24-hour infection time is appropriately justified to capture non-essential factors. However, the limited overlap with previous screens (only 4 common genes across all screens, C31) raises questions about reproducibility, though this is attributed to different experimental conditions.

results.result: G3BP1 was identified as a common hit across all three independent screening approaches (VPg proteomics, replication complex proteomics, and CRISPR screens), establishing it as a high-confidence host factor for norovirus infection.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is strongly supported by the convergence of three orthogonal approaches, each with independent validation. The identification of G3BP1 in all screens provides high confidence in its importance, though the claim itself is descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: G3BP1 is essential for MNV replication in BV2 cells. Three independent ΔG3BP1 clones showed severe defects in viral replication and cytopathic effect, while EMCV replication was unaffected, demonstrating specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by growth curves, cytopathic effect assays, and appropriate controls (Figure 4). The use of three independent knockout clones strengthens the conclusion, and the EMCV control demonstrates the defect is virus-specific rather than a general translation or cell viability issue. The conclusion (C38) appropriately summarizes the data.

results.result: G3BP1 is essential for human Norwalk virus (NV) replication. NV replicon RNA requires VPg for colony formation, and G3BP1 knockout in U2OS and BV2 cells completely abolished NV replication, which was restored by complementation with wild-type G3BP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 demonstrate G3BP1 requirement for human norovirus using multiple cell types and complementation. The proteinase K control (C39-C40) validates VPg-dependence, and the complete loss of colony formation and RNA synthesis in ΔG3BP1 cells (C41-C42) with restoration upon complementation (C43) provides strong evidence. The use of independently generated U2OS knockout cells (Kedersha et al., 2016) adds confidence.

results.result: The RNA-binding domains (RGG and RRM) of G3BP1 are essential for its function in the norovirus life cycle. Complementation with full-length G3BP1 restored MNV replication, while deletion of the RGG domain resulted in limited complementation, and deletion of both RGG and RRM domains completely abolished complementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by complementation experiments with defined G3BP1 truncations (Figure 6). The graded loss of function with progressive domain deletions (full-length > ΔRGG > ΔRGG/ΔRRM) provides strong evidence for the importance of RNA-binding domains. The conclusion (C48) is appropriately drawn from the data.

results.result: G3BP1 is required for a post-entry stage of the norovirus life cycle. Transfection of VPg-linked RNA into ΔG3BP1 cells resulted in no detectable viral proteins or infectious virus, comparable to polymerase inhibitor treatment, indicating a defect at a very early stage after entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 use RNA transfection to bypass entry and demonstrate G3BP1 functions post-entry. The comparison with 2CMC (polymerase inhibitor) provides appropriate context for the magnitude of the defect. The lack of detectable viral proteins (C50) and restoration by complementation (C51) support the conclusions. However, the inference about 'very early stage' (C50) is somewhat vague.

results.result: G3BP1 is required at or prior to viral negative-sense RNA synthesis. Both positive and negative-sense viral RNA synthesis were reduced to background levels in ΔG3BP1 cells during infection and after RNA transfection, and complementation with wild-type but not RNA-binding domain mutants restored RNA synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 use strand-specific RT-qPCR to demonstrate defects at the level of negative-strand synthesis. The detection of first-round negative-strand synthesis in WT cells treated with 2CMC (C56) validates assay sensitivity. The consistency between infection and transfection experiments, and the requirement for RNA-binding domains (C58), support the conclusions. The inference (C59) is appropriately cautious about whether G3BP1 functions 'prior to, or at the level of' negative-strand synthesis.

results.result: G3BP1 facilitates the association of VPg and viral RNA with ribosomal subunits. In the absence of G3BP1, VPg cannot efficiently pull down ribosomal proteins (RpS6, RpS3, RpL4), and viral RNA association with ribosomal protein RpS3 is decreased. This interaction requires both G3BP1 and the VPg-eIF4G interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 use GFP-Trap and RNA-IP experiments to demonstrate G3BP1's role in ribosome recruitment. The loss of ribosomal protein pulldown in ΔG3BP1 cells (C63) and with eIF4G-binding mutants (C64), and restoration upon G3BP1 complementation (C65), provide strong evidence. The RNA-IP data (C66) extends this to VPg-linked RNA. However, the authors acknowledge the relatively weak ribosome association in the GFP-Trap system and provide a reasonable explanation.

results.result: G3BP1 promotes polysome loading of norovirus VPg-linked RNA. In the absence of G3BP1, viral RNA is less efficiently recruited to polysomes during infection, even when viral RNA synthesis is inhibited, suggesting a defect in translation initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 use polysome profiling to demonstrate reduced polysome association of viral RNA in ΔG3BP1 cells (Figure 10). The use of 2CMC to inhibit RNA synthesis allows assessment of 'maiden round' translation. The observation of 80S accumulation in WT but not ΔG3BP1 cells (C68) is consistent with translation occurring in WT cells. The extended fractionation (C71) strengthens the conclusion. The inference (C72) appropriately summarizes the data.

results.result: G3BP1 specifically enhances norovirus VPg-dependent translation in vitro. Cell-free translation extracts from ΔG3BP1 cells showed normal cap-dependent and IRES-dependent translation but reduced VPg-dependent translation by ~40-50%, in both nuclease-treated and untreated extracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 use in vitro translation assays with appropriate controls (cap-dependent and CrPV IRES-dependent translation) to demonstrate specificity for VPg-dependent translation (Figure 11). The ~40-50% reduction is consistent across multiple experiments and conditions (nuclease-treated and untreated extracts). The quantification (C75) and consistency (C76) strengthen the conclusion. However, the partial rather than complete loss of translation differs from the in vivo phenotype, which may reflect differences between in vitro and in vivo systems.

results.result: G3BP1 plays a key role in norovirus VPg-dependent translation and is the first identified pan-norovirus host factor critical for both murine and human norovirus replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C79, C88, C130, and C131 are summary conclusions supported by the collective evidence from all experimental approaches. The demonstration of G3BP1 requirement for both MNV and human NV (C79, C131) across multiple assays establishes it as a pan-norovirus factor. The mechanistic link to VPg-dependent translation (C78, C88) is supported by multiple lines of evidence. These are appropriate summary statements of the major findings.

results.result: G3BP1 is a multifunctional protein involved in stress granule formation, RNA stability, translation regulation, and viral infection responses. Different viruses interact with G3BP1 and stress granules in distinct ways, either to promote replication or counteract antiviral effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 provide background context from the literature about G3BP1 function and virus-stress granule interactions. These are appropriately cited claims (C80-C87 all include citations) that establish the broader context for the study. While not original findings, they are accurately represented.

results.result: The RGG and RRM domains of G3BP1 are known to mediate 40S ribosome binding and stress granule formation, and these domains are required for G3BP1 function in norovirus VPg-dependent translation, confirming that 40S association is important for this role.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C91-C94 integrate established knowledge (C91-C92, citing Kedersha et al., 2016) with the current findings (C93) to draw a mechanistic conclusion (C94). The logic is sound: if RGG/RRM domains are required for 40S binding (established) and for norovirus function (demonstrated in C93), then 40S binding is important for norovirus function. However, C94 is an inference that assumes the only relevant function of these domains is 40S binding, which may be an oversimplification (acknowledged in C95-C96).

results.result: The interaction between VPg and G3BP1 is likely indirect and mediated through eIF4G, rather than through a direct binding motif. Unlike alphaviruses that use an FGDF motif to bind G3BP1, noroviruses lack a conserved G3BP1-binding motif, and the VPg-G3BP1 interaction is reduced by mutations in the eIF4G-binding domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C101 use sequence analysis (C99-C100) and functional data (C7, C11, referenced in C101) to argue for an indirect interaction. The lack of a conserved FGDF-like motif in human NV VPg (C100) and the dependence on eIF4G binding (C101) support this conclusion. However, the evidence is somewhat indirect—the authors do not directly test whether the interaction is mediated by eIF4G (e.g., by testing VPg-G3BP1 interaction in the absence of eIF4G).

results.result: G3BP1 may make multiple contacts with the 40S subunit and viral RNA genome, potentially contributing to additional functions beyond translation initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 are speculative (both marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type) and acknowledge this with language like 'it is possible' and 'may.' While the speculation is reasonable given that G3BP1 is enriched at sites of viral RNA synthesis (citing Brocard et al., 2018; Fritzlar et al., 2019), there is no direct experimental evidence in this study to support these additional functions. These are appropriate discussion points but not supported results.

results.result: BV2 murine microglial cells support human norovirus GI replicon replication, and this replication requires G3BP1. Complementation with wild-type G3BP1 partially restored replicon colony formation, confirming the machinery for HuNoV replication is conserved across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 extend the G3BP1 requirement to a different cell type and confirm species conservation (Figure 5D). The partial restoration (C108) is consistent with the lower efficiency of HuNoV replication in BV2 cells compared to BHK or U2OS cells (C106). The conclusion about conservation (C107) is appropriately drawn from the ability of mouse cells to support human virus replication.

results.result: Norovirus infection leads to preferential viral translation through multiple mechanisms including NS6 protease-mediated cleavage of PABP, apoptosis-induced cleavage of translation factors, and potentially NS3-mediated effects. The relative contribution of these mechanisms may vary by cell type.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 summarize previous work (C109-C114 all cite prior studies) and provide context for the current findings. The claims accurately represent the cited literature. C115-C116 are reasonable hypotheses based on the literature, though they are somewhat speculative (C115-C116 include SPECULATION in evidence_type). These provide important context but are not original findings of this study.

results.result: The differential enrichment of translation factors by NS1/2 versus NS4 may reflect distinct viral translation and replication complexes, or may result from NS1/2 being the first translated protein and serving as an anchor for translation complexes. The interaction may occur through an NS1/2-NS7-VPg complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 present alternative hypotheses to explain the differential enrichment observed in C20-C25. While the hypotheses are reasonable and based on established knowledge (C119-C121 cite previous work), they are largely speculative (C117, C118, C122 include SPECULATION in evidence_type). The authors appropriately acknowledge they 'cannot formally rule out other possible explanations' (C118). These are valuable discussion points but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: The norovirus replication complex is enriched for proteins involved in vesicle transport and lipid metabolism, consistent with its membrane-associated nature. NS1/2 and NS4 likely work together to regulate membrane-bound replication complex formation through interactions with multiple host factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C129 integrate the proteomic data (C18, C128) with established knowledge about NS4 function (C126, citing Doerflinger et al., 2017) and NS1/2-NS4 interactions (C129, citing Emmott et al., 2019). The gene ontology analysis (C18, C123) supports the enrichment of relevant pathways. However, C127 and C129 include speculative elements (SPECULATION in evidence_type) about regulatory mechanisms that are not directly tested. The overall conclusion is supported by the data, but the mechanistic details remain to be determined.

results.result: Targeting G3BP1 may hold future therapeutic potential for norovirus infections.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 is speculative (SPECULATION in evidence_type) and represents a potential application rather than a demonstrated result. While the essential role of G3BP1 in norovirus replication provides a rationale for this suggestion, there is no experimental evidence in this study regarding therapeutic targeting, potential toxicity, or feasibility. This is an appropriate discussion point but not a supported result.
